summary: For 9–10 year-olds, contrast sexual plant reproduction (pollination → fertilisation → seed, usually two parents, varied offspring) with asexual reproduction (runners, bulbs, cuttings, one parent, clones), and compare egg-laying with live-bearing animals. The load-bearing idea, kept age-appropriate without genes or alleles: the type of reproduction decides whether inherited features vary. Sexual reproduction mixes features, usually from two parents, so seed-grown offspring differ. Asexual reproduction copies one parent, so the offspring share the same inherited features. They may still differ in size or health because of growing conditions. This seeds KS3 variation and inheritance.
misconceptions: Thinking all plants reproduce only from seeds, not knowing about runners, bulbs and cuttings (asexual reproduction).
Believing offspring from a cutting or runner are the plant's 'children' that will differ, rather than identical clones.
Assuming only mammals reproduce, or that egg-laying animals aren't really reproducing.
Confusing pollination with fertilisation, or thinking a seed forms without pollen from another flower in sexual reproduction.

activities.title: Run both plant routes and compare the offspring
steps: Carry out the sexual route: move pollen from a flower on one plant to a flower on a different plant of the same kind (pollination). Use a diagram or model to follow the later, invisible step where cells join inside the ovule (fertilisation), which leads to seeds forming. Then grow the seeds into several sibling plants.

Carry out an asexual route from a SINGLE parent: peg down several runners from one strawberry plant, take several cuttings from one geranium, or plant offset bulbs split from one parent bulb. Grow the new plants alongside the parent in the same conditions.
Place the two sets of offspring side by side in a gallery: a row of seed-grown siblings versus a row of runner/cutting-grown plants.

Describe out loud or in writing what differs, focusing on inherited features such as leaf shape, leaf pattern or flower colour. Seed-siblings may vary in these features, while runner/cutting plants should match their parent. Size or health differences in either row can come from growing conditions.

State the rule the comparison reveals: sexual reproduction (usually two parents) → offspring with mixed, varied features; asexual reproduction (one parent) → offspring with the same inherited features as the parent (clones).
activities.insight: Whether offspring vary in inherited features depends on the type of reproduction. Sexual reproduction, usually with two parents, mixes features and produces variation. Asexual reproduction from one parent produces a copy with the same inherited features, though growing conditions can still change size or health. Genes are not needed to explain this.

activities.title: Label the flower and sequence the sexual route (reference / pre-teach)
steps: Identify and label stamen, stigma and ovary on a flower cross-section.
Put the sexual-reproduction steps in order: pollination → fertilisation → seed.
Sort example cards into asexual methods: strawberry runner, bulb, geranium cutting — naming each as producing a clone from one parent.
activities.insight: The processes and vocabulary of plant reproduction become crisp: the parts of a flower, the ordered pollination→fertilisation→seed sequence, and the familiar asexual methods.

activities.title: Compare egg-laying and live-bearing animals
steps: Follow an egg-laying example (bird, frog, many insects): lay and hatch an egg.
Follow a live-bearing example (most mammals): a live birth.
Sort familiar animals into egg-laying vs live-bearing groups.
Answer: is one of these 'more' reproduction than the other? (No — producing a new individual is reproduction whether by egg or live birth.)
activities.insight: Animals reproduce in different ways — egg-laying and live-bearing — and both are genuine reproduction; it is not only mammals that reproduce.

activities.title: Check and apply: why do gardeners take cuttings?
steps: Match examples to type: strawberry runner → asexual; apple seed → sexual.
Answer which offspring are identical to the parent, and explain why cuttings are clones.
Discuss or explain: a gardener takes a cutting to get a plant exactly like this one — why choose a cutting over a seed if you want two identical plants?
activities.insight: Applying the parent-number rule to a real purpose (cuttings for identical plants, seeds for variation) consolidates and extends the core idea.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A strawberry plant sends out a runner that grows into a whole new strawberry plant — no flower, no seed involved. Is that really reproduction? And will the new plant be identical to the parent or a bit different — how does that compare with a plant grown from a seed?'
checkAnswer: Yes — it is asexual reproduction: a new individual made from one parent without seeds or pollination. The runner plant is genetically identical to the parent (a clone). A seed-grown plant comes from sexual reproduction — pollination then fertilisation joins cells from two parents — so it varies from its parents.
